headline: Why the four-day week debate is really about trust
subheadline: Every argument about shorter working weeks eventually turns out to be an argument about whether managers believe their staff.
description: Column: The four-day week debate is framed as a question of productivity, but it is really a question of whether employers trust their employees.
author: e-novak

image.alt: An empty desk with a laptop, notebook and lamp after the working day
image.caption: An empty desk after hours (file photo). Trials of shorter working weeks have produced consistent results; the argument about them has not moved.

seo.title: Why the four-day week debate is really about trust | Opinion
seo.description: Column: strip away the productivity statistics and the four-day week debate is about whether managers believe their staff.

body: Every few months another trial of the four-day week reports its results, and every few months the same two camps restate the same two positions. Supporters cite lower burnout and stable output; sceptics cite the small sample sizes and the self-selection of companies that volunteer for such experiments.
Both are partly right, and neither is really talking about hours.

Strip away the statistics and the argument is about surveillance. A manager who believes work can be measured by presence will never be persuaded by a study. A manager who measures work by outcomes already knows that the fifth day is often the least productive.

body.text: The four-day week does not create trust. It reveals whether it was ever there.

body: This is why the debate is so stubborn. It is not that the evidence is weak; it is that the evidence answers a question most organisations are not actually asking.

Instead of asking whether a shorter week 'works', we might ask what it would take for a particular team to be judged on what it delivers. That conversation is harder, less quotable and far more useful. It is also the one a fan-owned football club in Meridian City apparently had with its players three seasons ago. Readers may have noticed how that turned out.

body.html: Elena Novak is a demonstration columnist for The Daily Meridian. Opinion pieces reflect the views of their authors and not necessarily those of the publication.
